P1.evidence: Weakest open of the batch. No notes or application read back. The frame was cut to two parts and delivered mid-chat — "go through where you're now at, where you want to go. See if we can help you bridge that gap" — dropping both the not-a-fit half and the what's-in-the-way element. No frame agreement was requested at all. The open question was replaced by "Well, let's talk about it, man. See if we can help you with that" after the prospect had already begun, so the scripted move never ran.

P2.evidence: The best baseline in the batch on the two things that were asked directly — "So how old are you at the moment?" and "How much do you currently weigh?" — though height was still skipped. The injury work was genuinely good: the 1-10 mobility scale was run, and when the answer felt incomplete the rep came back to it ("just to go back to that, because I didn't completely clarify on it"), which is what surfaced the jumper's knee, its seven-to-eight-month duration and the physiotherapy. Diet was worked thoroughly. But occupation came out only because the prospect volunteered dentistry and comedy, health conditions were never asked as a category, and sleep was never mentioned — on a man who works a clinical day job then does comedy at night, drives five hours to shows and reports being "always tired all the time".

P3.evidence: Deep and well run. "What is the best shape of Manish's life? How does that look?" opened it, and "It doesn't sound like this is only about the physical for you" bridged it to the real driver — mental sharpness for the comedy career. The rep pushed past a deflection when the prospect refused the pride framing ("What is there to be proud about?") and kept going. Two accurate reflect-backs, at 00:18:10 and 00:24:15. The gap is P3f: 'who else does that impact' was never asked. His wife appears only because he raised her at the very end, and she is both a co-decision-maker on a $6,000 purchase and someone independently trying to transform her own body — the single most valuable thread on the call and it was never pulled.

P4.evidence: The best-run phase anywhere in this batch, and it contains the single best move: the prospect tried to wave off his history with "you don't look at your past failures, right? That doesn't help you" and the rep refused to accept it — "Why do you think that they didn't work? Because if you don't look at it like that, then we're never going to be able to solve it." That produced the whole diagnosis in the prospect's own words: "I didn't know my why" and "the reason why it didn't work is because I was doing stuff that didn't sit with my mind." Past attempts, what happened, why it didn't stick and the structural gap all landed.

P5.evidence: The consequence question needed rewording — the prospect said "come again? I don't understand the question" — but unlike the Latham York call the rep rebuilt it successfully and it landed hard: "probably I'll just get heavier, probably just become sadder... I'll just continue until I'm like one of those 40 year old guys who have given up on life and they just complain about everything. I'll just become like one of those guys." The settle check followed immediately and produced "That is definitely not something I'm willing to settle for. No, no freaking way." The 'why not' follow-up was skipped and the line in the sand was asserted by the rep rather than requested.

P6.evidence: Correctly sequenced, and the lifetime version of the commitment was taken early at 00:19:12 — "you have to be willing to commit to yourself that you're going to work out three, four times a week... this is not a thing you do for six months and then drop off. So are you willing to also commit for the rest of your life?" / "Yeah. That's the whole point." The gap check ran at 00:31:43, before the presentation began at 00:33:26: "Is there anything from that that is missing in order to actually get to your goals?" / "Nah, man. Seems pretty good." A clear yes was in hand before anything was presented.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and every payment structure including the three-payment option was declined on cash availability ("To be honest, man, to be honest, no"), so payment and onboarding were never reachable.

objection_plays.detail: The closest anyone in this batch came to running the play. Isolation ran ("Outside of the finances, would you be like, yes, I want to do this?"), the HOW-not-SHOULD reframe ran almost verbatim and the prospect adopted it ("it sounds like it's more of a, how would I even make this possible, rather than, should I even do this?" / "Yeah, yeah, yeah. It's not, should I do this? It's how would I make it possible?"), the break-it-up move ran, and cash on hand was asked twice. What did not run: credit cards, total available credit, used versus available, and crypto, stocks or investments — four of the six financial-picture items. Given the prospect said his income is elastic ("if I need more money, I'll just work a bit more") and that he is a practising dentist, the credit and asset questions were the ones most likely to have found the first $2,000.

"I also need to have a chat with my wife about this as well... when you're married, you can't just make these kinds of decisions." The rep endorsed it — "definitely have that conversation with your partner about it... just make that decision together" — and ran no move at all. This was an unusually easy play: the prospect had already answered the key scripted question himself ("I don't think that she would say no, I think she would have no issue with this whatsoever. Because she also is trying to transform her body"), so the objection was self-defeating and was instead converted into a reason to delay.

"I think the best way would just be to save up." The rep did open correctly — "I wouldn't advise you to save up because it can take another six months without actually taking the action that you want to take" — which is the right instinct. He then abandoned it, agreed to the two to two-and-a-half month timeline, and offered to make monthly check-in calls. None of the scripted moves ran: nothing on things never slowing down, nothing on the only thing you can control being right now, nothing on the cost compounding.
"Let me just think about this man" and "I probably have to sit down and budget." Rep responded "I don't want to force you into doing anything right now" and moved to scheduling. No OA move ran.

Script gap, clinical. The prospect has a seven-to-eight-month patellar tendinopathy under active physiotherapy and asked the direct question the playbook has no answer for: "That's okay with the jumper's knee? It's gonna make it worse?" The rep answered "Yeah, it just comes down to building it up" and later promised "you're also not going to be able to injure yourself." Nothing in the script tells him to route that to the physiotherapist who is already treating it.

notes: Process-wise this is the strongest call in the batch after the Jake Brenner close — commitment before presentation, the best root-cause work anywhere here, and a consequence frame that recovered after a bad first phrasing. It lost on liquidity, which was knowable earlier: the rep never asked what the prospect earned or had, in an hour, until minute 51. Two coaching points independent of outcome. First, the wife was mentioned as a co-decision-maker who is herself trying to transform, and the rep neither ran OB nor explored the shared-goal angle. Second, and more serious than any adherence item: the rep told the prospect there were no payment plans and then produced four of them six minutes later, in two currencies.
